links.outcome: Perceived importance of AI-use information vs. radiologist consultation and standard surgery information
links.effect: AI use raised perceived importance of nearly all information items vs radiologist (e.g., 'AI used' mean diff -.2863, p<0.001); AI information rated more important than or similar to short-term effect information.
links.quote: This result provides support for a disclosure of information regarding AI use when AI is used in diagnosis.

links.outcome: Effect of procedure risk, AI prevalence, and AI superiority on perceived importance of AI information
links.effect: High risk raised importance only for opinion_same (b 0.0488, p=0.008) and reason_reject_accept (b 0.0434, p=0.02); commonness and superior performance had no significant effect.
links.quote: Surprisingly, neither the pervasiveness of the use of AI ( common ) nor the superior performance of the AI tool compared to an average radiologist ( superior ) had a significant effect on the perceived importance of AI information.

links.outcome: Patient-rated importance of information on AI capabilities, performance, and limitations
links.effect: Performance information (mean 5.87) and doctor experience with AI (5.89) rated significantly more important than short-term effect information (5.68); architecture rated among least important (5.59).
links.quote: The difference is either not statistically significant or the importance of AI information ( performance , doctor_experience and opinion_same ) was statistically significantly higher than the surgery information of short-term effect.

links.outcome: Perceived importance of the right to opt out of AI-assisted diagnosis
links.effect: Opt-out information was rated among the least important (mean 5.38 overall), though still high and rated higher under AI than radiologist (diff -.3335, p<.001).
links.quote: The two least important categories of information were the right to opt out from referring to a radiologist or AI decision support tool (mean score = 5.38) and architecture of the AI tool (mean score = 5.59).

links.outcome: importance of knowing whether AI was used in diagnosis
links.effect: ‘Used’ information: AI mean 5.6633 vs radiologist 5.3770; mean difference = -.2863, p < 0.001.
links.quote: For example, respondents perceived ‘whether a radiologist was referred to’ as less importantly than ‘whether an AI tool was used’ (mean difference = -.2863, p < 0.001).

links.effect: Performance diff −.1895 (P=.01), doctor_experience −.2098 (P=.005), opinion_same −.2443 (P=.001); used diff .0133 (P=.86).
links.quote: The difference is either not statistically significant or the importance of AI information ( performance , doctor_experience and opinion_same ) was statistically significantly higher than the surgery information of short-term effect.

links.outcome: risk, prevalence, and performance effects on disclosure preferences
links.effect: High_risk increased opinion_same b 0.0488, p = 0.008 and reason_reject_accept b 0.0434, p = 0.02; common and superior not significant.
links.quote: The perceived importance of AI information was for the most part not affected by the risk level of the operation, the wide-spread use of the AI tool, or whether the tool performed better than human physicians did.
